fullPassage: Many of us tend to have too much invested in our opinions of ourselves to see the world's feedback — the feedback we need to update our beliefs about reality. This creates a profound ignorance that keeps us banging our head against the wall over and over again. Our inability to learn from the world because of our ego happens for many reasons, but two are worth mentioning here. First, we're so afraid about what others will say about us that we fail to put our ideas out there and subject them to criticism. This way we can always be right. Second, if we do put our ideas out there and they are criticized, our ego steps in to protect us. We become invested in defending instead of upgrading our ideas. Emotional differences exist across ages, and there are ideal emotional paradigms for a given age (i.e., some emotions are reasonable at a given age), and these paradigms are realized and solidified with the help of normative group behaviors. For example, loudness, rudeness, and outbursts are associated with loss of self-control, and these emotions are often expressed among children. In childhood, crying is criticized but forgiven because it is consistent with the child's emotional profile, whereas in youth, crying is considered childish behavior. As individuals mature intellectually and increase self-control and social sensitivity, they gradually form emotions such as melancholy, sadness, etc. This shows the fact that some emotions can only be experienced at a certain age, and virtues such as integrity and wisdom are associated with certain stages of life (e.g., adulthood). The discovery that identities change the way we seek information raises interesting questions. For example, there is ample evidence that people try to make themselves look good in many situations. In contrast, researchers also found that people seek out negative information about themselves if it supports a negative identity. How is it that a person wants to make herself look good, while at the same time she wants to make herself look bad? Some researchers proposed that people try to obtain information that is consistent with their identities, whether they think of themselves positively or negatively. That is, people seek information that seems to them to be true, even if that information is negative about themselves. In contrast, positive information makes people feel good, whether it is consistent with their identity or not. Emotionally, people want to look as good as possible. One common misunderstanding of evolution is that it leads inexorably to organisms that are ever better designed. But Darwinian evolution is not a process of perfection. In contrast to the Lamarckian and Great Chain of Being theories of evolution, natural selection does not inexorably drive species up some kind of ladder of perfection. Rather, natural selection is, to borrow a term from economics, a process that leads to satisficing (just being "good enough for now"). In other words, so long as you survive and do better than your rivals, that is good enough. An antelope does not have to become the fastest animal on earth; it simply has to be faster than the lions that try to catch it. By the same token, lions and other predators do not have to be able to run marathons at top speed; nor do they have to be able to catch every prey animal. They just have to be fast enough to catch sufficient prey animals to survive.

questions.stem: 윗글의 흐름에 맞도록, 괄호 안의 단어를 어법에 맞게 변형하여 빈칸에 쓰시오. (한 단어로 쓸 것) (영어로)

det.korean: be동사(are) + 과거분사: 패러다임이 '실현되는' 수동태 → realize를 realized로.

questions.passage: Many of us tend to have too much invested in our opinions of ourselves to see the world's feedback — the feedback we need to update our beliefs about reality. This creates a profound ignorance that keeps us banging our head against the wall over and over again. Our inability to learn from the world because of our ego happens for many reasons, but two are worth mentioning here. First, we're so afraid about what others will say about us that we fail to put our ideas out there and subject them to criticism. This way we can always be right. Second, if we do put our ideas out there and they are criticized, our ego steps in to protect us. We become invested in defending instead of upgrading our ideas. Emotional differences exist across ages, and there are ideal emotional paradigms for a given age (i.e., some emotions are reasonable at a given age), and these paradigms are realized and solidified with the help of normative group behaviors. For example, loudness, rudeness, and outbursts are associated with loss of self-control, and these emotions are often expressed among children. In childhood, crying is criticized but forgiven because it is consistent with the child's emotional profile, whereas in youth, crying is considered childish behavior. As individuals mature intellectually and increase self-control and social sensitivity, they gradually form emotions such as melancholy, sadness, etc. This shows the fact that some emotions can only be experienced at a certain age, and virtues such as integrity and wisdom are associated with certain stages of life (e.g., adulthood). The discovery that identities change the way we seek information raises interesting questions. For example, there is ample evidence that people try to make themselves look good in many situations. In contrast, researchers also found that people seek out negative information about themselves if it supports a negative identity. How is it that a person wants to make herself look good, while at the same time she wants to make herself look bad? Some researchers proposed that people try to obtain information that is consistent with their identities, whether they think of themselves positively or negatively. That is, people seek information that seems to them to be true, even if that information is negative about themselves. In contrast, positive information makes people feel good, whether it is consistent with their identity or not. Emotionally, people want to look as good as possible. One common misunderstanding of evolution is that it leads inexorably to organisms that are ever better designed. But Darwinian evolution is not a process of perfection. In contrast to the Lamarckian and Great Chain of Being theories of evolution, natural selection does not inexorably drive species up some kind of ladder of perfection. Rather, natural selection is, to borrow a term from economics, a process that leads to satisficing (just being "good enough for now"). In other words, so long as you survive and do better than your rivals, that is good enough. An antelope does not have to become the fastest animal on earth; it simply has to be faster than the lions that try to catch it. By the same token, lions and other predators do not have to be able to run marathons at top speed; nor do they have to be able to catch every prey animal. They just have to be fast enough to catch sufficient prey animals to survive.
questions.stem: 윗글에서 다윈 진화(자연 선택)를 다루는 부분의 주제로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 자연 선택은 완벽이 아니라 생존에 충분한 수준(satisficing)을 향한다는 것이 해당 부분의 주제.
det.analysis:
❌ ① 멸종 위기 동물 보호 — 다루지 않음
❌ ② 경제학·생물학 공통점 — 용어 차용은 일부
❌ ③ 먹이사슬 관계 — 예시일 뿐
✅ ④ 진화는 완벽이 아니라 '충분히 좋음'을 향함 ←정답
det.tip: 진화 부분 주제 = good enough, not perfection

ch: 진화는 완벽이 아니라 생존에 '충분히 좋음'을 향한다는 점

questions.stem: 윗글에서 연령과 감정을 다루는 부분의 요지로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.korean: 연령별 이상적 감정 패러다임이 존재하고 성숙하며 복합 감정을 형성한다는 것이 해당 부분의 요지.
det.analysis:
✅ ① 연령에 따라 적절한 감정 전형이 있고 성숙과 함께 발달 ←정답
❌ ② 교육으로 안 바뀜 — 집단 행동으로 확고해진다고 함
❌ ③ 어느 나이나 유치 — 아동기는 용서받음
❌ ④ 미덕이 나이 무관 — 특정 단계(성인기)와 관련
det.tip: 감정 부분 요지 = 연령별 감정 전형 + 성숙 발달

ch: 감정에는 연령에 따라 적절하다고 여겨지는 전형이 있으며 성숙과 함께 발달한다.
감정은 타고나는 것이어서 교육으로 바뀌지 않는다.
미덕은 나이와 무관하게 누구나 갖출 수 있다.

questions.stem:
다음 우리말에 맞도록 [조건]을 이용하여 빈칸을 완성하시오.

"우리는 (우리의 생각을) 개선하기보다는 방어하는 데 공을 들이게 된다"의 일부:
We become invested __________ our ideas.

[조건] (1) defending, upgrading, instead, of, in 을 모두 사용
       (2) 정확히 5단어로 쓸 것 (영어로)

det.korean: in defending(방어하는 데) + instead of(~하기보다는) + upgrading(개선).
det.analysis: become invested in + 동명사(defending) / instead of + 동명사(upgrading).
det.tip: invested in defending instead of upgrading
